title: Dinoscript with Pip
subtitle: Write your first program, make three games, and solve math puzzles.
author: Francisco Claude-Faust
cover_alt: Pip, a little green triceratops with a yellow scarf, sits at a computer among ferns.
welcome: I'm Pip, a triceratops with three horns and a keyboard. Open Dinoscript and come learn with me. Each page gives you one small thing to type, run, or change.

pages.title: Make a dinosaur talk
pages.pip: My first program said hello. My second program asked for snacks.
body: Open Dinoscript. Type the line below in Code, or choose Try code when you read this page in the app.
Click Run or press F5. The word print tells Dinoscript to show something. The words between the double quotes show up in Output.
pages.challenge: Change the words between the quotes. Run it again. Can you make Pip introduce herself in two lines?
pages.hint: Try putting print("I am Pip!") on a new line under the first print.

checks.output: Hello, dinosaur!

pages.title: Give words and numbers a home
pages.pip: My bag has one sandwich and three rocks. Guess which I meant to pack.
body: Text in double quotes is called a string. A number goes in bare. Put commas between the pieces you want to print on one line.
A line starting with # is a comment. It's a note you can leave for the next person who reads the code. Dinoscript skips it.
pages.code:
# Pip checks her pockets.
print("Rocks in my pocket: ", 3)
print("If I pick up two more: ", 3 + 2)
pages.challenge: Put double quotes around 3 + 2 and run again. What changed? Then add a comment that tells me where the rocks came from.
pages.hint: With quotes, Dinoscript prints the characters 3 + 2. Without quotes, it adds and prints 5.

checks.output:
Rocks in my pocket: 3
If I pick up two more: 5

pages.title: Keep score with let
pages.pip: I can count berries on my claws. Beyond that, I need a variable.
body: A variable is a name for a value you want to keep. The first line puts 4 in a variable called berries.
The next line reads the value first, adds 3, and puts the new value back under the same name. The last line reads it again.
pages.code:
let berries = 4
let berries = berries + 3
print("I have ", berries, " berries.")
pages.challenge: Pip eats two berries before she counts them. Add a line above print that takes two away. What should the new total be?
pages.hint: Write let berries = berries - 2. You should see 5 berries.

checks.output: I have 7 berries.

pages.title: Ask for an answer
pages.pip: If you type 4, I promise I will count the four imaginary dinosaurs.
body: print asks the question. The empty parentheses in readint() tell you it takes no pieces of its own. It waits for you to type a whole number.
Click Run. When the input box lights up in Output, type your answer and press Enter. You can use Stop if your program is still waiting.
pages.challenge: Run with 4 guests. Then make each guest need three leaf plates. Try 0 guests, too.
pages.hint: With the original code, 4 guests need 8 plates. With three plates each, they need 12.

checks.output:
How many dinosaurs are coming?
We need 8 leaf plates.

How many dinosaurs are coming?
We need 0 leaf plates.

pages.title: Choose what happens
pages.pip: I can reach the picnic branch if I have at least two stepping stones.
body: if tests something that can be true or false. Here, >= means greater than or equal to. When the test is true, the lines after then run.
When the test is false, the lines after else run instead. end if closes the whole choice.
pages.code:
let stones = 2
if stones >= 2 then
  print("Across we go!")
else
  print("Find another stepping stone.")
end if
pages.challenge: Try 1, 2, and 3 stones. Can you predict which message each number will show?
pages.hint: With 1 you need another stone. With 2 or 3 you can cross.

checks.output: Across we go!

pages.title: Count fireflies with a loop
pages.pip: One, two, three, four, five. Please stay still, fireflies.
body: while checks its test before each trip through the block. The loop continues as long as the test is true.
The last line inside the loop changes fly, so the test eventually becomes false. You can click Stop if you forget to make the number change.
pages.code:
let fly = 1
while fly <= 5 do
  print("Firefly ", fly)
  let fly = fly + 1
end while
pages.challenge: Count backward from 5 to 1. Change where fly starts, the test, and the update.
pages.hint: Start at 5, use fly >= 1, and subtract 1 each trip.

checks.output:
Firefly 1
Firefly 2
Firefly 3
Firefly 4
Firefly 5

pages.title: Make your own command
pages.pip: A slope for three dinosaurs needs six bricks. I use that trick a lot.
body: A function is a few lines you give a name. bricksFor has one input, guests. Calling bricksFor(3) gives guests the value 3.
Inside a function, output sends a value back to the line that called it. print is how you show that value in the Output pane.
pages.code:
function bricksFor(guests)
  output guests * 2
end function

print(bricksFor(3))
print(bricksFor(5))
pages.challenge: Each dinosaur now needs two bricks and the ramp needs one extra. Change the function once to fix both answers.
pages.hint: Use output guests * 2 + 1. The two lines should say 7 and 11.

pages.title: Follow a bug to its hiding place
pages.pip: A bug is a clue. Some are small enough to hide behind one quote.
body: Run this program once. Then remove end if and run it again. Read the message in Output and click Go to error.
Dinoscript jumps to the line that starts the unfinished block. Put end if back below the print line, then run again.
pages.code:
let hungry = true
if hungry then
  print("Snack time!")
end if
pages.challenge: Next, remove the closing double quote on the print line. What does the new message ask you to fix?
pages.hint: Put the quote back after the exclamation point and before the closing parenthesis.

checks.output: Snack time!

pages.title: Fork in the Ferns
pages.pip: I packed a map. It says the fern on the left looks a lot like the fern on the right.
body: Use the numbers as buttons. The game waits for a choice and uses an if block to tell a different ending for each path.
pages.code:
print("1. Crystal trail")
print("2. Mossy cave")
let path = readint()
if path = 1 then
  print("You spot amber crystals!")
else
  if path = 2 then
    print("A shy bat shows you a secret door.")
  else
    print("The trail map only shows 1 and 2.")
  end if
end if
pages.challenge: Try 1, 2, and 9. Then make the bat ask a second question. What happens if the player says yes by typing 1?
pages.hint: Add a new print and readint() inside the cave branch, before its end if. Use another if to check the answer.

checks.output:
1. Crystal trail
2. Mossy cave
You spot amber crystals!

1. Crystal trail
2. Mossy cave
A shy bat shows you a secret door.

1. Crystal trail
2. Mossy cave
The trail map only shows 1 and 2.

pages.alt: Pip holds a map at a fork between amber crystals and a mossy cave.

pages.title: The Secret Fossil
pages.pip: I hid a fossil under a numbered rock. You get four guesses.
body: Every guess spends one turn. The loop keeps going while you have a turn left and found is false. Test both a win and a round that runs out of turns.
pages.code:
let secret = 7
let turns = 4
let found = false
print("Guess the fossil number from 1 to 10.")
while turns > 0 and not found do
  let guess = readint()
  if guess = secret then
    print("You found the fossil!")
    let found = true
  else
    if guess < secret then
      print("Too low.")
    else
      print("Too high.")
    end if
  end if
  let turns = turns - 1
end while
if not found then
  print("The fossil was under rock ", secret, ".")
end if
pages.challenge: Let someone change secret while the other player looks away. Can you add a message that shows how many turns are left?
pages.hint: Right after turns goes down, add print(turns, " turns left."). Put it in an if block if you want to hide it after a win.

checks.output:
Guess the fossil number from 1 to 10.
Too low.
Too high.
You found the fossil!

Guess the fossil number from 1 to 10.
Too low.
Too low.
Too low.
Too low.
The fossil was under rock 7.

pages.title: Pip's Snack Stand
pages.pip: Berry buns are three shells each. You have ten shells and an excellent appetite.
body: The function works out the bill. The shop checks for a negative order and tells you whether you can afford a valid one.
pages.code:
function bill(buns)
  output buns * 3
end function

let shells = 10
print("How many berry buns would you like?")
let order = readint()
let cost = bill(order)
if order < 0 then
  print("Order zero or more buns.")
else
  if cost <= shells then
    print("Buns: ", order)
    print("Shells left: ", shells - cost)
  else
    print("You need ", cost - shells, " more shells.")
  end if
end if
pages.challenge: Try to buy the most buns you can. Then invent a new snack with a different price. How does that change what you can afford?
pages.hint: Three buns cost 9 shells, so you have 1 shell left. Four cost 12, so you'll be 2 shells short.

checks.output:
How many berry buns would you like?
Buns: 3
Shells left: 1

How many berry buns would you like?
You need 2 more shells.

How many berry buns would you like?
Order zero or more buns.

pages.title: The egg baskets
pages.pip: I've got 23 eggs. My baskets hold four eggs each. Help me pack them.
body: Use // to count full groups and % to count what's left. Try to work out both answers for 23 eggs before you run the code.
pages.code:
let eggs = 23
let basketSize = 4
print("Full baskets: ", eggs // basketSize)
print("Eggs left: ", eggs % basketSize)
pages.challenge: For 23 eggs, find a basket size from 3 to 7 that leaves exactly 3 eggs over. Can you find two different sizes that work?
pages.hint: With sizes 4 and 5, the remainders are both 3. With size 4, there are 5 full baskets. With size 5, there are 4.

checks.output:
Full baskets: 5
Eggs left: 3

pages.alt: Pip sorts speckled eggs into baskets on a sunny picnic blanket.

pages.title: The stair of stones
pages.pip: I built stairs from pebbles. Step one has one pebble, step two has two, and so on.
body: This program adds each row to a running total. For four rows, it adds 1 + 2 + 3 + 4. The total is 10.
pages.code:
let rows = 4
let row = 1
let total = 0
while row <= rows do
  let total = total + row
  let row = row + 1
end while
print("Pebbles: ", total)
pages.challenge: You find a pile of exactly 28 pebbles. How many complete steps can you build? Find the number of rows with the program, then explain your answer to a friend.
pages.hint: Try 6 rows and then 7. Six rows take 21 pebbles and the next row takes 7 more.

checks.output: Pebbles: 10

pages.title: The fossil signal
pages.pip: Roar on a multiple of three. Stomp on a multiple of five. What about fifteen?
body: A number is a multiple of 3 when the remainder after dividing by 3 is zero. This starter catches Roar numbers. Add the Stomp and Roar Stomp rules.
pages.code:
let n = 1
while n <= 15 do
  if n % 3 = 0 then
    print("Roar")
  else
    print(n)
  end if
  let n = n + 1
end while
pages.challenge: Make 3 say Roar, 5 say Stomp, and 15 say Roar Stomp. Any number that matches neither rule should print as itself. Once it works, check 30.
pages.hint: First test n % 3 = 0 and n % 5 = 0 together with and. Only if that fails should you check the individual rules. At 30, you should get Roar Stomp.

1
2
Roar
4
5
Roar
7

Roar

Roar
